Let \(V=k^3\). A natural endomorphism of \(F=U^{\oplus 3}\) is the same thing as a \(3\times 3\) matrix with entries in \(A\), acting by left multiplication. Write an idempotent \(E\in M_3(A)\) as

\[
E=P e_{11}+Q e_{22}+R e_{33}+A_1a+B_1b+C_1c,
\]

with \(P,Q,R,A_1,B_1,C_1\in M_3(k)\). The idempotent condition gives

\[
P^2=P,\quad Q^2=Q,\quad R^2=R,
\]
\[
PA_1+A_1Q=A_1,\qquad QB_1+B_1R=B_1,
\]
\[
PC_1+A_1B_1+C_1R=C_1.
\]

The commutators simplify to

\[
D_a=(P+Q)a+B_1c,\qquad D_b=(Q+R)b+A_1c,\qquad D_c=(P+R)c,
\]

so

\[
D_aD_b=(P+Q)(Q+R)c.
\]

Since left multiplication by \(c=e_{13}\) on \(A\) has rank \(1\), evaluation on \(X_n=A^{\oplus n}\) multiplies the relevant \(3\times3\) matrix rank by \(n\). Hence

\[
\operatorname{rank}(D_aD_b)_{X_n}
=n\,\operatorname{rank}((P+Q)(Q+R)),
\]
\[
\operatorname{rank}(D_c)_{X_n}
=n\,\operatorname{rank}(P+R).
\]

Now \(P,Q,R\) are idempotent \(3\times3\) matrices over \(\mathbb F_2\). The first rank is at most \(3\), and rank \(3\) is attainable exactly when both \(P+Q\) and \(Q+R\) are invertible. For idempotents this forces

\[
\operatorname{rank}P+\operatorname{rank}Q=3,\qquad
\operatorname{rank}Q+\operatorname{rank}R=3,
\]

so \(\operatorname{rank}P=\operatorname{rank}R\). Thus \(P+R\) cannot be invertible; the best possible second rank is \(2\). Therefore

\[
(M_n,L_n)=(3n,2n).
\]

It remains to count.

There are \(28\) rank \(1\) idempotents and \(28\) rank \(2\) idempotents in \(M_3(\mathbb F_2)\). Fix a rank \(2\) idempotent \(Q\). The number of rank \(1\) idempotents \(P\) with \(P+Q\) invertible is \(10\). Among the \(10\) possible \(P\)’s and \(10\) possible \(R\)’s, exactly \(54\) ordered pairs satisfy \(\operatorname{rank}(P+R)=2\). Thus the rank pattern

\[
(\operatorname{rank}P,\operatorname{rank}Q,\operatorname{rank}R)=(1,2,1)
\]

contributes

\[
28\cdot 54=1512
\]

triples. By duality the pattern \((2,1,2)\) contributes another \(1512\). Hence there are

\[
3024
\]

maximizing triples \((P,Q,R)\).

For each maximizing triple, the equations for \(A_1\) and \(B_1\) each have \(2^5\) solutions. The final equation for \(C_1\) has a \(2^4\)-dimensional homogeneous solution space, and the term \(A_1B_1\) always lies in its image because the first two equations force the needed image/kernel inclusions. Thus each maximizing \((P,Q,R)\) lifts to

\[
2^5\cdot 2^5\cdot 2^4=2^{14}=16384
\]

natural idempotents \(E\). Therefore

\[
N_n=3024\cdot 16384=49\,545\,216.
\]

So for every \(n\ge 1\),

\[
\boxed{(M_n,L_n,N_n)=(3n,\;2n,\;49\,545\,216)}.
\]
